title: Element 3: Managing Risk — Understanding People and Processes
learningObjectives: Outline a systematic approach to conducting a risk assessment
Explain human factors that influence safe behaviour in the workplace
Describe common methods for identifying hazards
Explain how to select and implement appropriate risk controls

content.text: Risk assessment is the cornerstone of any effective H&S management system. It is a systematic process of identifying hazards, evaluating the risks they present, and deciding on appropriate control measures. A suitable and sufficient risk assessment has five steps.

rows: Identify the hazards
What could cause harm? Who might be harmed?
Decide who might be harmed and how
Workers, visitors, contractors, members of public?
Evaluate the risks and decide on controls
How likely is harm? How severe? What controls are needed?
Record the findings
Document hazards, risks, and controls; signed and dated
Review and update
When has something changed? After an incident? At least annually

items: Workplace inspections — Systematic walk-through observations of the work environment
Task analysis — Breaking work into individual steps and examining each for hazards
Job Hazard Analysis (JHA) / Task Risk Assessment (TRA) — Step-by-step hazard assessment for specific tasks
HAZOP (Hazard and Operability Study) — Formal technique for process plants; examines deviations from design intent
FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) — Examines how equipment could fail and the consequences
Accident and near miss investigation — Learning from past events
Consultation with workers — Those doing the job know the hazards best
Examination of data — Industry incident statistics, manufacturer's data sheets, research

content.text: NEBOSH exams frequently ask about suitable hazard identification methods. Know at least 4–5 with examples. JHA/TRA is the most common in Gulf industrial workplaces.

rows: Generic
For common, routine activities across multiple similar workplaces
Manual handling assessment for all warehouse workers
Site-Specific
Adapted from a generic assessment for a specific location or task
Generic manual handling RA modified for a specific confined storage area
Dynamic
Conducted in real time as conditions change during work
Fire fighter assessing a developing fire; soldier in combat situation

content.text: After identifying hazards, risk must be evaluated. The most common tool is the risk matrix, which plots Likelihood (probability) against Severity (consequence) to produce a risk rating.

rows: Critical / Intolerable
Stop work immediately. Do not proceed until risk is reduced.
High
Significant improvement required. Urgent action needed.
Medium
Controls must be improved. Set a deadline for action.
Low
Acceptable. Monitor and maintain existing controls.

content.text: Human factors (ergonomics in the broadest sense) are the environmental, organisational, job, and individual characteristics that influence behaviour in ways that can affect health and safety. Understanding human factors is essential for designing safe systems of work.

rows: Individual
Attitude, perception, knowledge, skill, risk tolerance, physical capability, fatigue, stress
Training gaps, fitness for work, mental health
Job
Task demands, workload, environment, tools, procedures, communication
Job design, ergonomics, shift work
Organisational
Culture, leadership, resources, communication, supervision, peer pressure
Safety culture, management systems, reporting culture

content.text: An action or omission by a person that fails to achieve the intended outcome. Types include: slips (attention failures), lapses (memory failures), mistakes (rule-based or knowledge-based failures), and violations (deliberate deviations from safe procedures).

items: Slips — Correct intention, wrong execution (e.g., pressing wrong button through habit)
Lapses — Correct intention, memory failure (e.g., forgetting a step in a procedure)
Mistakes — Wrong intention for the situation (e.g., misdiagnosing a problem and applying wrong fix)
Violations — Deliberate deviation from rules (routine shortcuts, situational exceptions, or sabotage)

content.text: Most accidents involve multiple contributing factors, not a single human error. The Swiss Cheese Model (Reason, 1990) illustrates how defences have holes (latent failures) that line up to allow an accident. Fixing one layer of Swiss cheese is not enough.

A formal procedure that defines a safe way to carry out a task. It results from a risk assessment and specifies: who does the work, what equipment is used, what controls are in place, what PPE is required, and the step-by-step sequence of operations.
Permit to Work (PTW) systems are a formalised type of SSoW used for high-risk activities where multiple controls must be verified before work starts. PTW is mandatory for:

items: Hot work (welding, cutting, grinding near flammables)
Work near pipelines carrying hazardous substances

content.text: The Permit to Work system is perhaps the most critical safety procedure in Gulf O&G operations. Aramco GI-0002.102 defines their PTW requirements in detail. Every HSE professional working on Aramco projects must understand PTW: the issuing authority's responsibilities, the concurrent works conflict check, the isolation certificate, and the closeout procedure. PTW failures have caused some of the Gulf region's worst industrial disasters.
